heading: PROPHET HŪD (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: STRENGTH WITHOUT ARROGANCE
themes: Tawḥīd • Humility • Gratitude • Service • Trust in Allah
scope: 6 CONNECTED STORIES | 10 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 10 DAILY ACTIONS
introduction: Volume Four continues ʿIBRAH Junior after the account of Prophet Nūḥ (AS). The last volume taught patience with purposeful effort; here Imaan, Akhlaq, Mohsin and Mohsina enter a five-day school competition that tests how they use their gifts. The story grows from their victories, boasts and mistakes into a Qur’anic lesson on the people of ʿĀd and the message of Prophet Hūd (AS).

The five substantial, previously developed Team Amanah stories—“Nobody Can Beat Us,” “Look What We Built,” “Who Gave You All This?,” “Strong Enough to Be Kind,” and “When Strength Was Not Enough”—are preserved as the narrative foundation. This edition adds a sixth original closing episode, a verified-verse working source library, ten independent app missions, answer keys, one daily action per mission and complete development guidance. The separate revised Imaan & Akhlaq Hūd story provides an editorial cross-check of themes and reported details.

blocks.text: The notice appeared on the main board of Sheikh Uncle’s Academy just after morning assembly: “Strength, Skills and Service Week — Five Days, Five Challenges, One Team Trophy.” Within minutes, the courtyard was full of excitement. There would be races, teamwork activities, construction challenges, problem-solving tasks and a final service project.

Akhlaq read the notice and immediately turned towards Imaan, Mohsin and Mohsina. “We are entering.” Imaan smiled and asked whether that was a suggestion. “A decision,” Akhlaq replied proudly. Mohsina laughed and reminded him that they had not even made a team yet. Akhlaq called that a technical detail. After several suggestions, including his rejected choice of The Unbeatables, they finally registered themselves as Team Amanah.

The first morning began on the school field with a relay challenge. Each member had a different task. Imaan crossed a narrow path while balancing a beanbag, Mohsina completed a quick puzzle, Mohsin carried a weighted bag between two markers, and Akhlaq finished with a sprint. The teacher reminded everyone that the competition was not only about speed. Dropping equipment, ignoring instructions or behaving unfairly would cost points.

The whistle blew. Team Amanah worked smoothly. Imaan stayed balanced, Mohsina solved her puzzle quickly, Mohsin carried the bag steadily, and Akhlaq raced through the final section. They finished first. “Alhamdulillah!” Imaan exclaimed. Mohsin grinned, while Akhlaq jumped in the air. Their happiness was natural. They had worked together and won fairly.

The next activity was tug-of-war. Mohsin looked at the rope and smiled. “Now this is interesting.” Team Amanah won the first round comfortably. The second round was much harder, but Mohsin encouraged everyone to pull together instead of at different times. Slowly the rope moved towards them. They won again. “Two competitions, two victories!” Akhlaq announced.

At lunchtime, a younger boy approached Mohsin and asked how he had carried the weighted bag so easily. Mohsin showed him how to hold it safely and encouraged him to practise. For now, winning had made them happy. It had not yet made them arrogant. But the third victory began to change something.

That afternoon, Team Amanah won an obstacle course as well. When another child congratulated them and said, “You people are impossible to catch,” Akhlaq laughed and replied, “You can still try.” Later, someone asked whether Team Amanah thought they would win the final trophy. “At this point,” Akhlaq replied, “you should probably ask who is coming second.” Mohsin burst out laughing. Even Imaan smiled. Mohsina did not. “That sounded a little proud,” she said. Akhlaq answered that he had been joking. Mohsina shrugged. “Nothing yet,” she said when he asked what was wrong.

The next morning brought another physical challenge, and Team Amanah again came first. Mohsin looked at the scoreboard with satisfaction. “I don’t think anyone here is stronger than us.” Akhlaq nodded. Imaan warned them not to become overconfident, but Mohsin pointed towards the scoreboard. “The numbers are right there.”

Nearby, a younger child was struggling to lift one of the practice bags. He tried once, dropped it, and tried again. Mohsin watched him and laughed. “That is going to take him all day.” The boy heard him. His face changed. Mohsina looked at Mohsin and told him he could help. Mohsin shrugged and said the boy would learn. Imaan glanced at him. Only one day earlier, his strength had made him useful to someone. Now the same strength was beginning to make someone else seem small.

The next event was different. Two team members had to carry a large lightweight box through a pathway without touching any cones. Because the box blocked their view, communication mattered more than physical strength. Akhlaq immediately chose himself and Mohsin because they were the strongest. Mohsina reminded him that it was a communication challenge.

Within seconds of starting, Akhlaq shouted, “Left!” Mohsin replied that he was going left. “Your other left!” Akhlaq yelled. The box struck a cone. Penalty. A few seconds later, they hit another. Another team moved much more slowly but communicated carefully and completed the course without touching anything. For the first time that week, Team Amanah did not win. They came third.

Akhlaq stared at the results and complained that the activity was badly designed. Imaan laughed and reminded him that all the activities had been excellent when they were winning. Mohsin complained that strength hardly mattered. Mohsina smiled and said, “Perhaps that was the point.” Despite the loss, Team Amanah still remained well ahead on the overall scoreboard.

As they headed towards the school gate, they passed the younger boy whom Mohsin had laughed at earlier. He was still practising with the training bag. This time he managed to lift it correctly. Mohsina smiled and praised him. The boy smiled back. Mohsin remained silent.

Near the gate, they found Zameer waiting beneath a tree. He asked how their competition was going. “We are winning,” Akhlaq replied immediately. “At the moment,” Imaan added. Zameer asked what they had learned. Akhlaq said that Mohsin was very strong and that he himself was very fast. Mohsina interrupted gently. “I think we are also changing.”

Zameer asked how. Mohsina thought for a moment. “On the first day we kept saying, ‘Alhamdulillah, we won.’ Today we keep saying, ‘Of course we won.’” Nobody laughed. Imaan slowly nodded. Mohsin shrugged and asked whether it was wrong to know that they were strong. “No,” Zameer replied. Being strong, talented or successful was not wrong. But he asked what happened when “I am strong” quietly became “I am better than you,” and when “we won today” became “nobody can beat us.”

Zameer sat on the bench and asked whether they knew of a people who became famous for their strength. Imaan immediately understood that another Prophet’s story was beginning. “The people of ‘Ad?” Zameer nodded. Allah had given the people of ‘Ad strength and many blessings, and He sent Hud (A.S.) to call them to worship Allah alone. Their strength itself was not the problem. The problem was what grew inside them because of it: arrogance.

Zameer told them that the Qur’an describes how ‘Ad behaved arrogantly on the earth without right. Their confidence in their strength became so great that they said, “Who is stronger than us in might?” Mohsin’s expression changed. Akhlaq slowly looked towards him. The words sounded very similar to what Mohsin had said that morning.

Zameer did not embarrass him. Instead, he asked who had given Mohsin his strength, health and opportunity to learn. Mohsin answered, “Allah.” Zameer explained that his strength was real, but it was also a gift. Akhlaq pointed towards the scoreboard and said that they had still worked to win. Zameer agreed. Humility did not mean pretending they had made no effort. The danger began when they remembered only what they achieved and forgot what they received.

Imaan repeated the thought softly: “Remembering what we achieved but forgetting what we received.” Mohsin looked towards the younger child with the training bag. “Yesterday my strength helped him. Today it made me laugh at him.” No one needed to explain further.

Zameer said, “Real confidence says, ‘Allah has given me an ability, so I will use it well.’ Arrogance says, ‘My ability makes me better than you.’” He gave them signs to watch for: enjoying someone else’s weakness, rejecting advice because they believed they knew better, expecting success because they felt superior, or speaking as if another person’s effort did not matter. Perhaps the most dangerous sign, he added, was becoming so impressed with oneself that one began forgetting Allah.

A few moments later, Mohsin looked across the field. The younger boy was trying to return the practice bag to storage. Mohsin stood, crossed the field and asked whether he wanted help. He showed him how to hold the bag properly, and together they carried it away. Akhlaq watched from beneath the tree. “He is still stronger than the boy,” he said. Zameer agreed. “But now his strength is useful.” Mohsina smiled. “That looks much better.”

Before leaving, Zameer told them that the following day would bring a construction challenge. Akhlaq’s eyes lit up. “We are very good at those.” Zameer raised an eyebrow. Akhlaq quickly corrected himself: “Allah has given us promising construction abilities.” Everyone laughed. Then Zameer became serious again. The people of ‘Ad, he said, were not only proud of their strength. Their power also appeared in what they built.

As the children walked home, the scoreboard still showed TEAM AMANAH — FIRST PLACE. Nothing had been taken from them. They were still talented and still leading. But now they understood that perhaps their greatest challenge was not remaining at the top of the scoreboard. It was remaining humble while standing there.

blocks.label: Challenge of the Day
blocks.text: Make Your Strength Useful
Choose one thing you are good at. Do not hide it and do not boast about it. Say: “Alhamdulillah, Allah has given me this ability.”
Then use that ability to help one person today. At the end, ask yourself: “Did my ability make someone feel smaller, or did it make me more useful?”
Level-Up

Watch yourself today for one warning sign of arrogance: laughing at someone’s weakness, refusing advice, expecting to be better than everyone, or looking down on another person. If you notice it, correct yourself immediately.
Confidence recognises the gift. Gratitude remembers the Giver. Arrogance begins when the gift makes us forget both.
Next Episode: Look What We Built

The construction challenge was the event Akhlaq had been waiting for. When the children entered the school hall the next morning, five large tables had been arranged across the room. Each table held cardboard, wooden sticks, paper tubes, string, tape, coloured sheets and other simple craft materials. At the front, the teacher announced the task: every team had ninety minutes to build a model of a small community centre. The structure had to stand on its own, include a useful public space and survive a simple stability test at the end.

Akhlaq looked at the materials and smiled. “This is ours.” Imaan immediately glanced at him. Akhlaq corrected himself. “InshaAllah, this is... potentially ours.” Mohsina laughed. “One lesson and already improving.”

The four quickly divided the work. Imaan sketched the basic design, Mohsina organised the materials, Mohsin worked on the stronger base, and Akhlaq took responsibility for assembling the taller sections. Their previous teamwork helped them enormously. While other teams were still deciding what to build, Team Amanah already had a plan.

Their model began taking shape surprisingly quickly. They created a wide entrance, a reading room, a small playground and a covered meeting area. Then Akhlaq had an idea. “What if we add a tower?” Mohsina asked why a community centre needed one. Akhlaq replied that it would look impressive. Mohsin liked the idea and suggested making it the tallest model there. Imaan hesitated, reminding them that the task was to make a useful community centre, not the tallest building. But there was nothing wrong with the tower itself, so they added it. Then Mohsin suggested another one.

Soon the simple community centre had two large towers, a decorative entrance and a raised platform. It looked impressive. Children from nearby teams began glancing towards it. One boy stopped beside their table and said, “Wow. That’s huge.” Akhlaq tried not to smile too proudly and replied that it was still unfinished. The boy looked at his own team’s much smaller model and walked away.

That was when something changed. Until then, Team Amanah had been concentrating on their work. Now they began concentrating on everyone else’s. Mohsin looked towards the next table and commented that their building was tiny. Akhlaq joked that perhaps it was the caretaker’s room. Imaan laughed before she could stop herself. The child working on that model heard them and looked down at his project.

Mohsina’s smile disappeared. She reminded Akhlaq that the child had heard him. Akhlaq said he was only joking. Mohsina replied, “You keep saying that.” A few minutes later, another team asked if they could borrow some tape. Their model was simple: one low building, a small library and a shaded garden. Akhlaq handed them the tape and asked whether they were keeping it that small. The girl explained that they wanted enough open space for children and elderly people. Akhlaq simply said, “Oh.” The way he said it made her uncomfortable.

Mohsina asked what was wrong with their idea. Akhlaq admitted there was nothing wrong. Imaan added that they had spent more time comparing their model with everyone else’s than improving their own. The teacher announced that only forty minutes remained, and the four returned to work.

Their final model was easily one of the largest in the hall. The two towers rose above nearly every other project. When the teacher came by, she praised their workmanship. Several other children gathered around. Someone said Team Amanah was definitely winning again. Another pointed towards the towers and said nobody else had built anything like that. The praise felt good. Perhaps too good.

By the time judging began, Akhlaq was no longer wondering whether their model met the requirements. He was wondering how many people were looking at it. The first team presented a small community centre with a wheelchair ramp and a garden. Mohsina whispered that it was thoughtful. Akhlaq replied that it was very simple. The second team had built a rainwater collection system. Imaan was impressed, but Mohsin said their building still looked much better.

Then came Team Amanah’s turn. Akhlaq explained the meeting hall, reading space and playground. Mohsina described how families could use the community area, and Imaan explained the layout. Then the teacher pointed towards the two towers and asked what purpose they served. Nobody answered immediately. Akhlaq finally said, “They make the building look important.” Mohsin added, “And taller.” The teacher smiled gently and asked if there was anything else. For the first time, Akhlaq realised they had spent almost a third of their time building something that had no real purpose.

The stability test began. Each model had to remain standing while the table was gently shaken. Team Amanah’s strong base held well, but one of the tall towers swayed dangerously. Mohsin reached towards it, but the teacher stopped him because no touching was allowed during the test. The tower leaned, then stopped. It remained standing. Their model passed. But so did the smaller model Akhlaq had joked about. Its low design barely moved.

When the results were announced, Team Amanah won the award for Best Craftsmanship. They did not win the overall construction challenge. That went to the team with the smaller community centre, because their design had been judged the most useful, accessible and appropriate to the task.

Akhlaq stared at the result. “But ours was much more impressive.” Mohsina reminded him that this had not been the only requirement. Mohsin complained that the winning team had barely built half as much as they had. The girl who had borrowed their tape heard him, and her smile faded. Imaan noticed and asked why their success had to become an insult to Team Amanah’s work. Nobody answered.

A familiar voice came from behind them. “Perhaps because sometimes we stop building something useful and begin building our own importance.” They turned and saw Zameer. Akhlaq looked towards the model and said that Zameer always arrived at inconvenient moments. Zameer admired the model and asked what the towers were for. Akhlaq sighed, while Mohsina explained what had happened.

Zameer said that the previous day they had spoken about the people of ‘Ad and their pride in strength. Today they had reached another part of Hud’s warning. In Surah Ash-Shu‘ara, Hud (A.S.) challenged his people about the way they built. The Qur’an describes them constructing on elevated places structures or landmarks for display, and making strong buildings as though they might remain forever.

Akhlaq immediately asked whether building was wrong. Zameer said no. Building useful homes and structures was not arrogance. Creating something beautiful was not automatically arrogance either. The Qur’anic passage pointed towards attitude: wasteful display, pride and the illusion that power could last forever. The problem was when what they built became a way of declaring how great they were.

Imaan looked towards the winning model. “They built less, but thought more about who would use it.” Zameer agreed and asked why Team Amanah had built the towers. Akhlaq answered quietly that they wanted everyone to look at them. Zameer said the towers themselves were not the real issue; the reason mattered. What had been happening inside them while they built?

Mohsin admitted that they had started thinking that because their project was bigger, everyone else’s was worse. Mohsina added that they had begun treating people that way. Zameer explained that arrogance often hides inside comparison. A person receives something good, but instead of asking, “What can I do with this?” they begin asking, “Who has less than me?” The blessing itself may be good, but the heart can turn it into a ladder for standing above other people.

Akhlaq asked whether they should stop trying to make impressive things. Zameer told them not at all. They should make excellent things, build beautifully and work creatively. Humility did not require laziness. The question was: “Am I improving the work, or am I using the work to enlarge myself?”

The question was harder than it sounded. Imaan thought about how much she had enjoyed the praise. Mohsin remembered dismissing the winning team. Akhlaq remembered the little “Oh” he had given the girl. Mohsina had noticed the arrogance earlier than the others, but another uncomfortable thought entered her mind: she had begun feeling proud of the fact that she was the one who had noticed it.

Zameer noticed her expression. Mohsina admitted that she had been thinking that at least she was not behaving like the others, and then realised she was starting to feel better than all of them because she was more humble. Zameer laughed and called that one of arrogance’s cleverest hiding places. The humour helped them understand that arrogance was not limited to loud boasting. A person could become proud of intelligence, strength, possessions, religious knowledge, kindness, leadership or even humility itself.

Before leaving, Team Amanah walked towards the group that had won the challenge. Akhlaq told them that their design deserved to win. Mohsin admitted that the ramp and garden were better ideas than their towers. The girl smiled and said their towers had still looked amazing. Akhlaq laughed and said that they mostly provided emotional support. Imaan congratulated them, and Mohsina asked how they had designed the wheelchair access.

Within minutes, both teams were discussing ideas rather than comparing themselves. Team Amanah had not become less talented. Their model had not become less impressive. But perhaps they were beginning to understand that achievement did not require someone else to become smaller. Hud (A.S.) was beginning to teach them a lesson the people of ‘Ad had refused to learn: no building was tall enough to make the person who built it greater than everyone else.

blocks.label: Challenge of the Day
blocks.text: Create Without Comparing

Make or complete something today — a drawing, school assignment, model, piece of writing, organised space or any useful task. Try to make it excellent, but do not compare it with someone else’s work merely to feel superior.
When you finish, ask: “Did I make this better because I wanted to do good work, or because I wanted to prove that I am better?”
Level-Up
Find one good quality in the work of someone whose achievement is smaller, simpler or different from yours, and genuinely appreciate it.
Excellence says, “How can I improve my work?” Arrogance says, “How can I prove my work is better than yours?”
Next Episode: Who Gave You All This?

By the third day of Strength, Skills and Service Week, Team Amanah had learned two uncomfortable lessons. First, being strong did not make them better than anyone else. Second, building something impressive did not give them permission to look down on simpler work. Akhlaq had decided that this meant the safest thing to do was win quietly. Mohsin looked at him and asked, “You? Quietly?” Akhlaq replied that he was developing.

The next challenge was called The Problem-Solving Mission. Each team had to build a working bridge from limited materials and use it to move a small container safely across a gap. The bridge would be judged for stability, planning, teamwork and efficient use of resources.

As soon as the materials were distributed, Team Amanah began confidently. Their teacher, Ms. Sana, had spent part of the previous afternoon showing the class how triangular supports could strengthen a structure. Mohsin remembered the demonstration immediately. They decided to use triangles underneath the bridge while Mohsina sorted the materials and Akhlaq drew a quick plan.

Ten minutes later, they discovered a problem. Their longest wooden strips were too short to cross the gap. Ms. Sana reminded them that they could not have more materials. Then Bilal, who was passing through the hall with another group, stopped beside them and suggested overlapping two strips and supporting the join underneath. The four children tested the idea. It worked.

Later, the school caretaker found them searching for a way to stop their bridge from sliding on the smooth table. He suggested placing small rubber pieces underneath the base. Mohsina tried it, and the movement almost disappeared.

By the final twenty minutes, their bridge was standing firmly. They had used Ms. Sana’s lesson, Bilal’s joining idea, the caretaker’s rubber support and their own teamwork to create one of the strongest designs in the room. When testing began, Team Amanah’s bridge held the container perfectly. More weight was added. It bent slightly but remained standing. The room burst into applause. Team Amanah had won.

Akhlaq smiled widely but remembered his new rule. He turned towards his teammates and whispered, “Quiet celebration.” Mohsin nodded seriously, and both of them silently punched the air. Imaan laughed.

After the judging, several children gathered around the bridge. One asked how they had made it so strong. Mohsin began explaining the triangular supports. Another asked how they had joined the short pieces. Akhlaq pointed proudly towards the centre. “We solved that.” Mohsina looked at him and reminded him that Bilal had suggested it. Akhlaq paused, then said that they had developed it.

A teacher from another class came by and praised the design. “You four have done excellent work.” Akhlaq smiled. “Thank you. We did everything ourselves.” Mohsina turned towards him so quickly that he noticed. She asked, “Everything?”

Akhlaq looked confused. Mohsin nodded and said that they had built it. Imaan looked at the bridge, then at the triangular supports and rubber pieces beneath the base. She slowly raised an eyebrow. “Did we?” Mohsina began counting on her fingers. Ms. Sana had taught the triangular support, Bilal had suggested overlapping the strips, and the caretaker had given them the rubber idea. The school had provided the materials, the teachers had given them time to practise, and Allah had given them hands, minds, health and the ability to learn.
Akhlaq looked at the bridge again. “Perhaps ‘everything ourselves’ was slightly inaccurate.”

That afternoon, the results board was updated. Team Amanah remained in first place. A younger child nearby heard them talking and said, “You are lucky.” Akhlaq immediately replied, “It isn’t luck. We worked for it.” The child shrugged and walked away. Imaan looked at Akhlaq. He was right that they had worked, but he sounded as if effort were the only reason anything had happened.

A familiar voice behind them asked, “Who told you gratitude requires denying your effort?” They turned and saw Zameer. Akhlaq smiled and said they had another argument for him. They showed him the winning bridge and explained what had happened.

Zameer asked whether they had worked hard, planned and made decisions. They answered yes. He explained that acknowledging Allah’s blessings did not erase any of that. The problem with saying they had done everything themselves was that the word “ourselves” removed everyone and everything that had made their effort possible.

He asked Akhlaq to imagine attempting the same challenge without the teacher who taught them, without materials, without health, without time, without the ability to understand instructions and without the people who had helped when they were stuck. Akhlaq became quiet. Zameer explained that they had made a real effort, but their effort had grown inside a field of blessings.

Zameer said this was something Hud (A.S.) repeatedly reminded his people about. The people of ‘Ad had not created their own strength. Allah had given them blessings, power and opportunities. In Surah Al-A‘raf, Hud (A.S.) reminded them that Allah had made them successors after the people of Nuh and increased them in strength and stature, then instructed them to remember the favours of Allah so that they might succeed.

Mohsin observed that even when Hud (A.S.) spoke about their strength, he connected it back to Allah. Zameer agreed. He then explained that in Surah Ash-Shu‘ara, Hud (A.S.) reminded his people of the One who had provided them with what they knew: livestock, children, gardens and springs. Mohsina said that in a way, he was making them count their blessings. Zameer agreed that he was reminding them that their lives were full of things they had received.

Akhlaq asked whether someone who worked harder than everyone else still deserved credit. Zameer said yes. Gratitude did not mean saying, “I did nothing.” It meant saying, “I worked, but I was able to work because Allah gave me means, opportunities and abilities.”

Mohsina walked towards the bridge and pointed to its parts. One came from Ms. Sana’s lesson, one from Bilal and another from the caretaker. Akhlaq realised they should thank them. Zameer added that recognising people’s contribution was part of good character.

First they found Ms. Sana and thanked her for the lesson on triangular support. Then they found Bilal and told him that his overlapping idea had helped them win. Finally, they thanked the caretaker for his suggestion. By the time they returned, something about their victory felt different. They were still proud of their work, but they were no longer pretending the bridge had appeared from four completely independent minds.
Akhlaq stared at the scoreboard again and said that first place still looked nice. Imaan laughed. Zameer agreed that a blessing should produce gratitude, not shame.

Mohsin asked why the people of ‘Ad had failed to see this. Zameer explained that when blessings continue for a long time, people can begin treating them as if they were owed. Health becomes “of course I am healthy.” Wealth becomes “of course I have this.” Talent becomes “of course I am better.” Strength becomes “of course nobody can defeat us.”

Imaan remembered the difference between their first and second day. First they had said, “Alhamdulillah, we won.” Later they had said, “Of course we won.” Zameer nodded. There was a great difference between those two sentences.

Akhlaq looked at the bridge and said that perhaps gratitude was what stopped success from becoming arrogance. Zameer agreed and gave them a question to remember whenever they felt proud of something: “What did I contribute, and what did I receive?” Both questions mattered. If they remembered only what they received, they might become lazy and refuse responsibility. But if they remembered only what they contributed, they might become arrogant.

Before leaving school, Team Amanah placed a small card beside their bridge for the exhibition. At first Akhlaq wrote BUILT BY TEAM AMANAH. Then he stopped and added: With thanks to our teachers, helpers and everyone who shared an idea. Alhamdulillah for the ability to learn and work together.

The bridge had not become smaller. Their victory had not disappeared. Their effort still mattered. But now the achievement pointed beyond themselves. As they walked away, Zameer told them that the next lesson would be about what happened when people stopped using blessings merely to admire themselves and began using strength to control others. “So tomorrow is not about what we have,” Mohsina said. Zameer nodded. “It is about what we do with it.”

blocks.label: Challenge of the Day
blocks.text: Count What You Received
Choose one achievement you are proud of today. It might be a good mark, a sporting ability, something you made, a skill you learned or a responsibility you completed.

First say what you contributed: practice, effort, patience, planning or discipline. Then name at least three things you received that helped you: health, parents, teachers, time, knowledge, opportunity, materials or someone’s advice.
Finish by saying: “Alhamdulillah for what Allah gave me, and Alhamdulillah that He allowed me to use it.”
Level-Up
Thank one person whose contribution to your success is easy to overlook.
Arrogance remembers only, “I achieved.” Gratitude also remembers, “I received.”

By the fourth day of Strength, Skills and Service Week, Team Amanah had become the team everyone recognised. They were still leading the scoreboard, their bridge had won the previous day’s challenge, and even younger students had begun watching them with admiration.

That morning, however, Ms. Sana announced something unexpected. “Today there is no competition between your teams.” Akhlaq immediately looked concerned. No competition, trophy points or rankings? Ms. Sana smiled and explained that it was the Service Challenge. Each senior team would be paired with a group of younger children. Their job was to help them complete three activities: organise a reading corner, prepare care packs for the school support staff, and create a simple teamwork game.

Akhlaq slowly raised his hand and asked whether this meant they were in charge. Ms. Sana corrected him: they were responsible for helping. Akhlaq smiled and claimed that this was what he had meant. Mohsina whispered that it absolutely was not.

Team Amanah was paired with six younger children. At first, everything went well. Imaan explained the reading-corner task, Mohsina helped sort books, Mohsin carried the heavier boxes, and Akhlaq began assigning jobs. One little boy said he wanted to make the labels. Akhlaq told him no, because he was faster at carrying books. The boy looked disappointed but obeyed.

Across the room, Mohsin saw two younger children struggling with a box. “Move,” he said. “I’ll do it.” They stepped aside. Mohsin lifted the box easily and carried it across the room. One of the children followed and asked whether they could help. Mohsin replied that he had already done it. The child became quiet.

A few minutes later, Imaan noticed that the books were being arranged very slowly. She told a younger girl to stop arranging them by subject and instead put large books in one place and small ones in another because it would be faster. The girl removed the books she had already organised. Mohsina watched from across the room. Something did not feel right. Team Amanah was completing the tasks quickly, but the younger children were hardly doing anything.

During the second activity, the children had to prepare thank-you packs for the school guards, cleaners and other support staff. Each pack contained a handwritten card and a few simple items provided by the school. Mohsina suggested letting the younger children decide what to write. Akhlaq looked at the clock and said they would take forever.

One younger boy heard him and insisted they would not. Akhlaq told him to show them. The child started writing carefully. After a minute, Akhlaq leaned over his shoulder and corrected a spelling mistake. Then he said the letters were too big. By the third correction, the boy put the pencil down and said, “You write it.” Akhlaq took the pencil. Mohsina immediately stepped in and told him to give it back.

Akhlaq said he was trying to make sure the work was good. Mohsina asked what the boy was learning. Nearby, Mohsin had taken over the job of carrying nearly every pack, and Imaan was rewriting labels because she wanted them to look neater. Mohsina looked around and said, “We were supposed to help them do the work.” Mohsin replied that they were helping because they were finishing everything. “That is not the same thing,” Mohsina answered.

For the first time that day, they realised that the younger children looked less excited than when they had started. One girl was simply sitting with her hands folded. Another child had stopped offering ideas. They were completing the challenge, but doing it almost entirely by themselves.

During the break, Team Amanah sat beneath the tree outside the hall. Akhlaq was still bothered. Their work had been fast and neat, so what had been wrong? A familiar voice came from behind them. “Perhaps nothing was wrong with the work. Perhaps the problem was what your strength and authority were doing to other people.” They turned and saw Zameer.

Mohsina explained what had happened. Zameer asked Mohsin why he had carried every heavy box. Mohsin said it was because he could. Zameer asked whether the younger children could have carried any of them safely together. Mohsin admitted they could. Then Zameer asked what his strength had taught them. Mohsin hesitated and answered, “That I am stronger?”

Zameer then asked Imaan why she had rearranged the books. She said her method was faster. Was the younger girl’s method wrong? Imaan admitted that it was not. Finally, Zameer asked Akhlaq why he had decided everyone’s job. Akhlaq said someone needed to lead. Zameer asked whether leadership required deciding everything. Akhlaq became quiet.

Zameer said that the previous day Hud (A.S.) had reminded his people that their blessings came from Allah. But the Qur’an showed another serious problem among the people of ‘Ad: how they used power. In Surah Ash-Shu‘ara, Hud (A.S.) criticised their harsh, tyrannical use of strength, asking, “And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.”

The children became silent. Akhlaq asked whether they had hurt people. Zameer immediately clarified that their small mistake was not equal to the tyranny of ‘Ad. It was not. But the story warned them about where pride in power could lead. Strength could change from helping to controlling.

Zameer pointed out that the previous day Mohsin’s strength had helped a younger child carry something. Today the same strength had told younger children, “Move. I can do this better than you.” Imaan realised that she had thought her faster method meant everyone had to follow it. Akhlaq admitted that he had thought being responsible meant everyone had to follow his decisions.

Zameer explained that there was an important difference between leadership and control. “A leader uses strength to help other people become capable. A controlling person uses strength to make other people dependent.” Mohsin looked towards the hall. Without intending to, they had made the younger children dependent.

Akhlaq asked what real strength looked like. Zameer explained that sometimes it meant lifting the box, but sometimes it meant standing beside someone while they learned to lift it safely. Sometimes leadership meant giving instructions, but sometimes it meant listening. Sometimes being clever meant solving the problem, but sometimes it meant helping someone else discover the answer.

Mohsina smiled. “So strong people should make other people stronger.” Zameer said that was a good way to remember it. Akhlaq asked what they should do now. Zameer told them to go back and help the younger children finish the work themselves.

When Team Amanah returned to the hall, Akhlaq went first to the boy whose card he had taken. He placed the pencil in front of him and admitted that he had been correcting too much. The boy asked what would happen if he spelled something wrong. Akhlaq replied that he could help if asked. This time, Akhlaq sat beside him instead of over him. When the child misspelled a word, Akhlaq quietly asked whether he wanted help. The boy nodded. It took longer, but when the card was finished, the child smiled proudly.

Across the room, Mohsin returned to the boxes. Two younger children asked whether they could carry one. He showed them how to stand on opposite sides and lift together. The box rose and moved slowly. Akhlaq joked that at this speed they might finish next Thursday, then immediately corrected himself and said they were developing valuable skills. Everyone laughed.

Imaan returned to the girl organising books and asked her to show her idea again. The girl explained that she wanted stories on one shelf, information books on another and picture books where younger students could reach them easily. Imaan listened and admitted that it was actually better than her own idea. Together they made labels.

By the final activity, the atmosphere had completely changed. Instead of creating the teamwork game themselves, Team Amanah asked the younger children for ideas. One suggested a ball-passing game, another wanted clues, and a third wanted everyone to have a turn leading. They combined the ideas into a simple activity. This time, Team Amanah did not lead the game. The younger children did.

When the bell rang, Ms. Sana saw handwritten cards with imperfect letters, a reading corner arranged partly by children, and six younger students excitedly explaining the game they had created. She asked who had done all this. Akhlaq opened his mouth, then stopped and looked at the younger children. “They did.” One boy pointed at Team Amanah and added, “They helped us.”

As everyone packed up, Mohsin told Zameer that he thought he understood Hud’s lesson better. Strength should not make people afraid of what he could do; it should make them feel safer because he was there. Mohsina added that leadership should not mean making everyone smaller so she could look bigger. Imaan said that if she knew more, she should help someone learn, not make them feel foolish.

Akhlaq thought for a moment and said that if he was in charge, perhaps the question was not, “How much can I make people obey me?” but “How much better can people become because I led them well?” Zameer nodded.

Before leaving, Zameer reminded them that the final day was coming. Their bridge, construction model and service projects would all be displayed in the courtyard. Akhlaq smiled at the return to competition. Mohsina asked what lesson was left. Zameer looked towards the sky, where a steady breeze moved through the trees. “What happens when people become so confident in their strength that they begin to believe nothing can bring them down?” For once, Akhlaq did not joke.

blocks.label: Challenge of the Day
blocks.text: Use Your Strength to Make Someone Stronger
Choose one situation today in which you know more, can do more, are older, stronger or have more authority than someone else.
Instead of taking over, help that person learn to do something themselves. Ask: “Am I helping because I am stronger, or controlling because I am stronger?”
Level-Up
If you are given leadership today, practise these three actions: listen before deciding, explain instead of ordering when possible, and give someone else a chance to contribute.
Arrogance uses strength to dominate. Good character uses strength to protect, teach and serve.
Next Episode: When Strength Was Not Enough

The final morning of Strength, Skills and Service Week arrived with more excitement than any of the previous days. The school courtyard had been turned into an exhibition area. Team Amanah’s bridge stood on one table, their community-centre model on another, and photographs from the service challenge had been placed on a display board nearby. By lunchtime, parents, teachers and students would walk through the courtyard before the final trophy was announced.

Akhlaq stood in front of their display with his hands on his hips and said that it looked excellent. Imaan smiled. “Alhamdulillah, it does.” Mohsin pressed gently against the base of their tall community-centre model and said it was strong. Mohsina looked towards the two decorative towers and asked whether it was strong enough. Mohsin replied confidently that it was.

Just then, Ms. Sana approached. A steady breeze had begun moving through the courtyard, lifting the corners of some posters. She checked several displays and asked the teams to make sure that nothing tall or lightweight could fall. When she reached Team Amanah’s table, she examined their model and suggested securing the towers more firmly. Mohsin tested the base and said they were fine. Ms. Sana pointed out that the wind was getting stronger and advised them to reinforce it with tape and support sticks.

After she moved away, Imaan reached for the tape. Akhlaq asked whether they really needed to rebuild part of it now. Mohsin pressed the model once more and called it solid. Mohsina reminded them that Ms. Sana had told them to strengthen it. Akhlaq replied that she thought they should, while they thought it was fine. The model really did look strong, so they left it.

The exhibition began shortly before midday. Children moved from table to table. Parents admired the projects, and teachers asked questions about what each team had learned during the week. Team Amanah received plenty of praise. One parent admired their bridge. Another complimented the community-centre model. A younger student pointed at the towers and whispered that theirs was the biggest. Akhlaq heard him, smiled, then caught himself and quietly said, “Alhamdulillah.” Mohsina noticed and smiled too. Perhaps they really had changed.

The wind, however, continued to grow stronger. One paper sign blew across the courtyard. Several teams began holding down their displays. Imaan looked towards their model and suggested securing it now. Mohsin glanced at the crowd and said the presentation started in five minutes. Akhlaq worried that taping it now would make it look as if something were wrong. Mohsina stared at him. “So?” Akhlaq hesitated. That answer sounded worse once it had left his mouth.

Before he could say anything else, a sudden gust of wind swept through the courtyard. The display cloth lifted. One of their signs fell flat. Then the taller tower on their model moved. Mohsin reached towards it, but he was too late. The tower leaned sideways, pulled part of the upper structure with it and fell onto the empty section of the table. Everyone nearby stepped back. Nobody was hurt.

For a few seconds, Team Amanah simply stared. Their beautiful model was damaged. Akhlaq looked at the fallen tower. “But it was strong.” Mohsina replied quietly, “Not strong enough for this.” Ms. Sana came over, checked that everyone was safe and helped move the loose pieces away. She did not scold them. Akhlaq admitted that they should have listened. Mohsin said he had thought that because he tested it with his hand, he knew. Imaan looked at the unused support sticks and said they had everything they needed to strengthen it; they had simply thought they did not need to.

A familiar voice behind them said, “Sometimes the most dangerous words are not ‘I cannot.’ They are ‘nothing can happen to me.’” They turned and saw Zameer. He first asked whether everyone was all right. When they said yes, he reminded them that a model could be repaired.

Akhlaq said that it had been supposed to be their best display. Zameer replied that it might now have given them the most important lesson of the week. Mohsin looked at the fallen tower and asked whether this was about ‘Ad. Zameer nodded, but immediately clarified that their tower had fallen because of an ordinary gust of wind and because it had not been secured properly. This was not a punishment from Allah, and they should not compare a school model falling with what happened to the people of ‘Ad. It could simply help them understand that feeling strong did not mean having no limits.

Zameer reminded them that Hud (A.S.) had called his people to worship Allah alone, reminded them of Allah’s favours and warned them against arrogance. Yet many of them continued to reject him. They had become so impressed with their strength that the Qur’an records their boast: “Who is stronger than us in might?” Mohsin remembered Episode One. The words no longer sounded impressive. They sounded dangerous.

Imaan asked what happened next. Zameer explained that eventually Allah’s decree came. The Qur’an describes how the people of ‘Ad saw something approaching like a cloud towards their valleys. They thought it was bringing rain. Mohsina was surprised. Zameer explained that they had misunderstood what they were seeing. It was the punishment they had demanded impatiently.

The punishment came through a tremendously powerful, bitter wind. In another Qur’anic passage, Allah tells us that it continued against them for seven nights and eight days. Mohsin looked towards the trees moving in the courtyard breeze. The people of ‘Ad had been proud of their strength, yet they could not stop the wind. No worldly strength could protect them from Allah’s decree.

Zameer continued that Hud (A.S.) had never taught them that strength was useless. He taught them that their strength was not independent of Allah. Imaan understood the difference. It was one thing to say, “Allah gave us strength,” and another to say, “Our strength means we do not need Allah.”

Mohsin asked what happened to Hud (A.S.) and the people who believed. Zameer told them that the Qur’an says Allah saved Hud (A.S.) and those who believed with him by His mercy. Akhlaq noticed the wording. They had not been saved because they were physically stronger, because their buildings were better or because they had more people. They were saved by Allah’s mercy.

The children remembered the lessons of the entire week. Strength had not been the problem. Achievement had not been the problem. Building had not been the problem. Leadership had not been the problem. The problem began when blessings were turned into evidence of superiority and independence.

Mohsina said that the people of ‘Ad had gifts, but the gifts had not made them humble. Zameer agreed. A blessing could bring a person closer to Allah through gratitude, or become a test when it made the person admire themselves.

Akhlaq looked down and asked what he should do if he won. Zameer said to thank Allah. If he lost, he should still thank Allah and learn. If he was strong, he should use the strength well. If he was weak at something, he should learn without feeling worthless. Mohsin added that if someone else was weaker, he should help them. Imaan said that if they built something good, they could enjoy it without needing another person’s work to look bad. Mohsina added that if someone gave them good advice, they should not ignore it just because they were confident. Akhlaq looked at the fallen tower and said that one felt unnecessarily specific. Everyone laughed.

The trophy announcement took place later that afternoon. Team Amanah stood with the other teams while Ms. Sana reviewed the week. She praised not only winning, but teamwork, improvement, service, honesty and the way students had responded to mistakes. Then she announced the overall result. Team Amanah had won.

For half a second, Akhlaq’s mouth opened as if a huge celebration was about to come out. Then he looked at Mohsin, Imaan and Mohsina. Together they smiled. “Alhamdulillah,” Akhlaq said. This time the words did not feel like something they had remembered to say. They meant them.

When the trophy was handed to them, Akhlaq held it for a few seconds and then passed it to the younger children who had worked with them during the service challenge. One of them said that they had not won the competition. Akhlaq smiled. “You helped us learn how to.”

Later, as the children packed up their damaged model, Mohsin decided not to throw away the fallen tower. Imaan asked what he was doing with it. He said he was keeping it as a reminder that being strong and being unstoppable were not the same thing. Imaan added that being successful and being independent of Allah were definitely not the same thing.

Akhlaq picked up the trophy and asked what real strength was. Zameer, who had returned to say goodbye, heard the question. “Real strength,” he said, “is receiving Allah’s blessings without allowing them to make you forget Him.”

The children looked at the trophy, the repaired bridge, the damaged tower and the younger students helping pack the hall. They had begun the week wanting to prove that nobody could beat them. They finished it understanding something far more valuable. There would always be someone stronger, faster or cleverer, and even the greatest human strength had limits. Humility did not make a person smaller. It taught them where their strength truly came from.

blocks.label: Challenge of the Day
blocks.text: Turn Pride into Gratitude
Think of one blessing that sometimes makes you feel proud: your intelligence, strength, appearance, possessions, marks, popularity, family, talent or achievements.
Say: “Alhamdulillah. Allah gave me this blessing, and I am responsible for how I use it.” Then use that blessing in one way that benefits someone else.
Level-Up
When you succeed, practise three steps: thank Allah, appreciate the people who helped you, and ask how you can use the success responsibly.
Confidence says, “I can try.” Arrogance says, “I cannot fall.” Humility says, “Whatever strength I have is from Allah.”

stories.title: The Quietest Victory
stories.subtitle: What becomes of a trophy when the week is over?

blocks.text: The trophy stood in the centre of the living-room table, surrounded by the certificates that Team Amanah had received. Under the bright lamp it looked more impressive than it had at school. Akhlaq had already photographed it twice, and Mohsin had sent a cheerful message to their group: “Champions!”
“Are you taking another picture?” Imaan asked as Akhlaq moved the trophy a little to the left.
“I am improving the lighting.”
“Of course. The trophy deserves professional attention.”
Dadi Jaan entered with a small tray of dates. She admired the trophy, said “Mā shāʾ Allāh,” and then asked a question nobody expected. “What will happen to it next week?”
Akhlaq looked puzzled. “It will still be a trophy.”
“And you will still be the winners?”
“We won fairly,” he answered.
“Yes,” Dadi said. “But what will the victory do?”

The question followed them to school the next morning. The scoreboard had been taken down. The cardboard models were packed away, and the excitement of Strength, Skills and Service Week was already fading. A few children still congratulated Team Amanah, but most were talking about the coming science fair.

Near the library, Imaan noticed the young boy who had struggled with the training bag earlier in the week. He was carrying a stack of books nearly as tall as his chest. Mohsin stepped towards him before anyone asked. “Let me help,” he said, lifting half the books.
Akhlaq grinned. “Our strongest team member has joined the library transport department.”

“Excellent career opportunity,” Mohsin replied. But he looked pleased in a different way from the day he had first carried the winning bag. The younger boy walked beside him without looking embarrassed.

At lunchtime, the team gathered with Sir Zameer in the library. On a table lay two cards. One said WHAT WE WON. The other said WHAT WE GAVE. Under the first, the teacher placed a picture of their trophy. Under the second, nothing had been written.
“Which card should be longer?” Sir Zameer asked.
“The first!” Akhlaq said. “We won a lot.”
“Then perhaps you should read the second card at the end of the day.”

He reminded them that Prophet Hūd, peace be upon him, had not called his people to despise the blessings Allah had given them. Their strength, gardens, children and abilities were gifts. But gifts brought duties. The people of ʿĀd refused the guidance of their Lord and acted as though their strength could make them independent. Allah saved Hūd and those who believed with him by His mercy. That truth, Sir Zameer said, should make a person grateful rather than boastful.
Imaan looked at the two cards. “We have practised talking about gratitude,” she said. “Maybe the second card is for doing something.”

They spent the afternoon planning a small library corner for younger pupils. Mohsina suggested picture labels so new readers could find the shelves. Imaan designed a tidy borrowing sheet. Mohsin offered to move the heavy books, and Akhlaq volunteered to teach the new pupils how to use the lending system. Everyone contributed something different.

When one student suggested placing their trophy beside the library corner, Akhlaq hesitated. He imagined how many people would look at it. Then he remembered the model’s tall towers and the uncomfortable way he had spoken about other teams.
“We can leave the trophy in the cabinet,” he said. “The little ones need space for books, not a display about us.”

That evening the WHAT WE GAVE card was no longer empty. It contained the names of tasks rather than the names of heroes: books organized, students helped, labels prepared, younger readers welcomed. Sir Zameer read it quietly and placed it beside the photograph of the trophy.
“Which will matter longer?” he asked.
Akhlaq considered the question. “The trophy shows that we were successful once. The service shows what we did with it.”

At home, Dadi Jaan opened the wooden box that had started so many of their earlier journeys. From it she took a small smooth stone. No words were written on the stone, but there was a folded card underneath. Imaan opened it.
“Another people. Another test. A warning that power does not excuse disobedience.”
Akhlaq stared at the stone. “Another Prophet?”
Dadi smiled. “We will open that journey next time. For now, tell me the greatest thing you learned from Prophet Hūd.”
Imaan answered first. “Allah is the One who grants blessings, and He alone deserves worship.”
Mohsin said, “Being strong does not give me permission to look down on anyone.”
Mohsina added, “A beautiful thing is more beautiful when it helps someone.”
Akhlaq glanced at the trophy one final time. “And winning is not the end of the responsibility.”

Dadi closed the box. The trophy remained on the shelf. In the school library, new readers would soon open books that Team Amanah had helped place within their reach. One prize would gather dust; the other good work could keep helping people.

missions.title: A Gift Called Strength

discover.label: Character focus
discover.text: Gratitude and responsible ability

discover.label: Learning outcome
discover.text: Name one ability, recognize it as a gift, and use it to help someone.
READ & UNDERSTAND — The Qur’anic lesson

Hūd (AS) reminded his people that Allah had made them successors after the people of Nūḥ and increased them in bodily strength. In the Qur’anic setting, this reminder was part of a call to worship Allah, remember His favours and stop rejecting His guidance. Strength was not evil in itself. A people may possess health, resources and influence, yet become forgetful of Allah. The lesson is therefore not to be weak but to be grateful and accountable. When a child runs quickly, understands maths easily or communicates confidently, that gift brings an opportunity to serve others. A person should not deny real effort or talent; the mistake is treating ability as proof that other people matter less.
DISCOVER — The modern situation
After a relay victory, Mohsin notices a younger pupil struggling with a bag. Akhlaq wants to celebrate and move on. Mohsina asks what their strength is for.

evidence.arabic: أَوَعَجِبْتُمْ أَنْ جَاءَكُمْ ذِكْرٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ عَلَىٰ رَجُلٍ مِنْكُمْ لِيُنْذِرَكُمْ ۚ وَاذْكُرُوا إِذْ جَعَلَكُمْ خُلَفَاءَ مِنْ بَعْدِ قَوْمِ نُوحٍ وَزَادَكُمْ فِي الْخَلْقِ بَسْطَةً ۖ فَاذْكُرُوا آلَاءَ اللَّهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ
evidence.meaning: Hūd reminded his people of their place after Nūḥ’s people, their great strength, and Allah’s many favours.

choices.feedback: Right. Talent can be enjoyed while also becoming useful to others.

missions.title: Who Is Stronger Than Us?

discover.label: Character focus
discover.text: Humility and avoiding pride

discover.label: Learning outcome
discover.text: Recognize a boastful comparison and replace it with grateful confidence.
READ & UNDERSTAND — The Qur’anic lesson

Allah records that the people of ʿĀd acted arrogantly on the earth and boasted about their strength, asking who could be stronger than they were. The verse answers by reminding them that Allah, their Creator, is stronger. Their error lay in self-glorification and denial of Allah’s signs, not merely in being physically capable. Children may feel pleased when they win; genuine delight is not prohibited. Yet rejoicing can become arrogance if victory leads to contempt for other learners or a refusal to accept correction. Humility means seeing our capabilities truthfully while remembering that Allah bestowed them and can test us through them. We can celebrate a win, admit limits and still praise another team’s effort.
DISCOVER — The modern situation
Team Amanah wins three games. A classmate calls them unbeatable, and Akhlaq is tempted to announce that nobody else deserves to compete.

evidence.arabic: فَأَمَّا عَادٌ فَاسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ وَقَالُوا مَنْ أَشَدُّ مِنَّا قُوَّةً ۖ أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَهُمْ هُوَ أَشَدُّ مِنْهُمْ قُوَّةً ۖ وَكَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يَجْحَدُونَ
evidence.meaning: ʿĀd boasted, “Who is stronger than us?” but Allah, who created them, has greater power.

missions.question: Which reply shows confident humility?

choices.text: We worked hard, alḥamdulillāh; other teams are improving too.
choices.feedback: Right. Gratitude and honest effort can stand together.

choices.text: Everyone else is weak, so we should always win.
choices.feedback: This makes other people small and treats current success as permanent superiority.

choices.text: We must never try to win again.
choices.feedback: The lesson forbids arrogance, not effort or healthy competition.

missions.title: The Message That Comes Before the Prize

discover.label: Character focus
discover.text: Tawḥīd and recognizing guidance

discover.label: Learning outcome
discover.text: Explain in simple words the central message of Prophet Hūd (AS).
READ & UNDERSTAND — The Qur’anic lesson

Before the lessons about buildings, strength and wind, the Qur’an tells us why Hūd was sent. He called his people to worship Allah alone and reject invented false claims about gods besides Him. This Tawḥīd is the central teaching; the character lessons flow from it. The people of ʿĀd possessed real worldly blessings but had turned away from the One who gave them. In our fictional world, Imaan and Akhlaq might be absorbed by a school prize, but a trophy must not take the place of remembering Allah and doing what is right. The classroom comparison is only an application. We must never suggest that modern school mistakes are equivalent to the people’s rejection of their Prophet.
DISCOVER — The modern situation
Before presenting their model, Akhlaq can think only about the trophy. Imaan asks whether their work has a worthwhile purpose and whether they have remembered Allah.

evidence.arabic: وَإِلَىٰ عَادٍ أَخَاهُمْ هُودًا ۗ قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مَا لَكُمْ مِنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرُهُ ۚ أَفَلَا تَتَّقُونَ
evidence.meaning: Allah sent Hūd to the people of ʿĀd to tell them to worship Allah alone and be mindful of Him.

evidence.arabic: وَإِلَىٰ عَادٍ أَخَاهُمْ هُودًا ۚ قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مَا لَكُمْ مِنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرُهُ ۖ إِنْ أَنْتُمْ إِلَّا مُفْتَرُونَ
evidence.meaning: Hūd called the people of ʿĀd to worship Allah alone and reject fabricated claims about other gods.

choices.feedback: A prize is temporary, and right conduct should not be sacrificed for it.

choices.text: Winning proves Allah is pleased with us.
choices.feedback: A worldly prize does not reveal anyone’s rank before Allah.

choices.text: Worship Allah alone, act honestly and do work that benefits people.
choices.feedback: Right. Faith and ethical duties guide what we pursue.
